segments.text: Let us begin this chapter with the smallest building block of everything that follows: the ordered pair, where the position of each entry actually carries meaning.

<curious> Imagine a chaiwala near a railway platform. He sells three sizes, small, medium and large, and two flavours, adrak and elaichi. Before ordering, ask yourself: how many genuinely different cups can he serve?

You instinctively start pairing. Small adrak, small elaichi, medium adrak, medium elaichi, large adrak, large elaichi. Six cups. Taking every item from one list and tagging it with every item from the second list is the entire idea we are building toward.
Each cup is really a pair with two slots. The first slot holds a size, the second holds a flavour, and the two slots play completely different roles. That is what mathematicians call an ordered pair.

Here is the crucial warning. A cup written as small comma adrak is a size paired with a flavour. Flip it and you are reading a flavour paired with a size, a different kind of label entirely. We are never allowed to swap slots casually.

Think of a cricket scoreline written as runs comma wickets. One eighty for four means one hundred eighty runs for the loss of four wickets. Read it backwards and you are claiming four runs for one hundred eighty wickets, which is nonsense. Same numbers, opposite meaning.
So we lock this in formally. Two ordered pairs are equal exactly when both coordinates match in their own slots: a equals c and b equals d. Both conditions, each in its own position.

One immediate consequence: the pair a comma b equals the pair b comma a only in the special case where a and b are the same element. Whenever they differ, the two pairs are genuinely different objects.
Now the definition writes itself. We give the two lists names, call the sizes set A and the flavours set B, and collect all possible cups into one set.

Given two non-empty sets A and B, the Cartesian product A cross B is the set of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate is pulled from A and whose second coordinate is pulled from B. Nothing more, nothing less: every possible pairing, gathered into one set.
We read the symbol aloud as A cross B. The rule of membership is rigid: the first slot must be filled from A, the second slot from B. That slot discipline is the entire content of the definition.

Picture it as a grid. List the elements of A up the side, the elements of B along the bottom. Every element of A meets every element of B at exactly one intersection point, and those six green meeting points, labelled with their ordered pairs, are precisely the set A cross B.
What about B cross A? There the first slot is filled from B and the second from A, flavours-then-sizes in our chai picture. Both products carry the same information, but packaged in opposite slots.
And because order inside a pair is rigid, those are different sets. In general A cross B is not equal to B cross A. Hold on to this; it is one of the most tested facts of the whole subtopic.

One beautiful special case. If both A and B are the set of real numbers, then R cross R is the set of all pairs x comma y, which is exactly every point of the coordinate plane. The XY-plane you have drawn since childhood is itself a Cartesian product, and Descartes' name is attached to both for the same reason.
Before we compute anything, a few boundary rules are worth nailing down, because examiners love hiding traps exactly at these edges.

First, the empty set collapses everything. If either A or B is empty, there is simply no way to form even a single pair, so the whole product A cross B is the empty set. And the arrow runs both ways: the product is empty exactly when at least one factor is empty.

Think of assembling a pair as picking one part from each of two shelves. If one shelf holds nothing, assembly is impossible, no matter how rich the other shelf is. Spotting this instantly saves you from wasting exam time on pointless pairing.
Second, infinity persists. If one of the sets is infinite and the other is non-empty, the product is infinite too. That is exactly why R cross R, the coordinate plane, has uncountably many points.

Third, a quiet assumption behind counting. The clean product rule for counting pairs assumes the elements within each set are distinct. Sets never repeat elements anyway, but a problem may hand you a list with repeats, and you must strip duplicates before you count.
Finally, the equality question. For non-empty sets, A cross B equals B cross A exactly when A and B are the same set, because only then do both slots draw from the same pool.

A subset relation is not enough. Take A containing just one and B containing one and two: the pair one comma two lives in A cross B, but two comma one does not, so the products differ. Containment is weaker than equality, and this distractor appears in papers again and again.
This section is your formula sheet for the Cartesian product. Everything here gets used constantly, so let us walk through each entry and what it says.

The counting rule first. If A has p elements and B has q elements, both finite, then A cross B has exactly p times q pairs. Every element of A pairs with every element of B, so the count multiplies, it never adds.

The membership test. A pair x comma y belongs to A cross B exactly when x belongs to A and y belongs to B, each coordinate checked against its own set. This one line settles every is-it-in-or-not question.

The idea extends beyond two sets. The product of n sets consists of ordered n-tuples, one coordinate from each set in order, and the count is simply the product of all the individual sizes. For the m-fold product of A with itself, the count is n of A raised to the power m.

For two sets the tuples are ordered pairs, for three they are ordered triples. R cubed, the triple product of the reals, is exactly three dimensional space, every point an ordered triple of coordinates.
Now the bridge formula. Since A cross B holds p q elements, the number of its subsets is two raised to the power p q. Each pair independently gets a yes or a no, and those binary choices multiply.
<whisper> Remember this one especially, because each such subset is about to be christened a relation from A to B. This single formula is the bridge into the next subtopic.

Finally, the product distributes over set operations: A cross the intersection of B and C equals the intersection of the two products, and the same pattern holds for union and difference. The star identity for speed questions is the last one: the intersection of A cross B with C cross D equals A intersect C, cross, B intersect D.

Let $A = \{a_1, \ldots, a_m\}$ and $B = \{b_1, \ldots, b_n\}$. Claim: $n(A \times B) = mn$.

segments.text: The counting formula deserves a real proof, because it is the reasoning, not the formula, that protects you in a trap. The argument is called slicing, and it will reappear later in this chapter.
Write the elements explicitly. A has m elements, a one through a m, and B has n elements, b one through b n. We claim the product has exactly m times n pairs.

Fix one element a i of A, and gather every pair whose first coordinate is that a i. That collection is the singleton a i crossed with B: the pairs a i with b one, a i with b two, all the way to a i with b n.
Why group this way? Because every pair in the product has exactly one first coordinate, so this slicing sorts all pairs into clean, separate groups, with nothing left over and nothing double counted.
Now count one slice. The slice for a i has exactly as many pairs as B has elements, namely n, one pair for each choice of second coordinate.

Next, the slices never overlap. For two different first coordinates, a pair cannot simultaneously start with a i and with a k, so the two slices share nothing. This disjointness is what licenses us to simply add their sizes.
The finish. There are m slices, each of size n, all disjoint, and together they cover every pair. So the total is n added to itself m times, which is m times n. Proof complete.
Step back and notice what we proved: this is just the multiplication principle of counting dressed in set notation. m independent choices followed by n independent choices give m times n outcomes.
Now the second theorem worth proving in full: the Cartesian product distributes over intersection. Boards and JEE both lean on this identity, so let us see exactly why it holds.
The standard way to prove two sets equal is to show each is a subset of the other. Here we can do both directions at once with a single chain of biconditionals, where every step reverses.
Take an arbitrary pair x comma y in A cross the intersection of B and C. By the membership test, this means x is in A, and y is in B intersect C, which unpacks to y in B and y in C.

Now regroup: x in A and y in B, together with x in A and y in C. But those two bracketed statements are exactly membership in A cross B and membership in A cross C, so the pair lies in the intersection of the two products. Every arrow reverses, so both sets contain exactly the same pairs. Proof complete.

The lone subtle move is the regrouping, where we duplicated the condition x in A so it could attach to each branch. That works because x in A, and, P and Q, is logically identical to, x in A and P, and, x in A and Q. The distributive law of logic mirrors the distributive law of sets.
One more tool before examples: a favourite exam manoeuvre runs the definition backwards. You are handed the finished product and asked to recover the original sets.
The procedure is mechanical. Collect the first entry of every ordered pair; the distinct values form A. Then collect the second entry of every pair; the distinct values form B.

Always finish with the sanity check: the size of A times the size of B must equal the number of pairs you were given. If it does not match, either a pair is missing from the list, or the set you were handed was never a genuine Cartesian product.

segments.text: Time to put the machinery to work. First a board-level example: A holds two, three and five, B holds the letters x and y. We want both products, the count, and a verification that they differ.

For A cross B, the first coordinate comes from A. Pair every number with every letter: two with x, two with y, three with x, three with y, five with x, five with y. Six pairs, written out systematically so nothing is missed.

For B cross A the slots flip: now every letter leads. x with two, x with three, x with five, then y with two, y with three, y with five. Again six pairs, but look at their shape, letter first, number second.

The count confirms: three elements times two elements is six, matching what we listed. And to verify the products differ, one witness is enough: the pair two comma x lives in A cross B, but in B cross A the first coordinate must come from B, so it cannot appear there. Different sets.

Now a JEE speed trap. A holds one and two, B holds one, two and three. How many ordered pairs are common to A cross B and B cross A? Brute-force listing is slow, and the reflex answer zero, from remembering the products are unequal, is flat wrong.

The one-line weapon is the star identity from our formula sheet. Intersecting A cross B with B cross A gives A intersect B, cross, B intersect A, and both brackets are the same set, so the overlap is A intersect B crossed with itself.

Here A intersect B is the set containing one and two, with two elements. So the common pairs form a two by two grid, four pairs in total: one one, one two, two one, and two two. One line, no enumeration.

<excited> Note the lesson carefully: unequal products can still overlap. The overlap count is always the square of the size of A intersect B. Lock that in, it converts a two minute question into a ten second one.

Two harder examples now, each linking several ideas at once. First: the product A cross A has sixteen elements, and we are told two of them, one comma four, and three comma two. Find A, then count subsets containing the pair four comma one.

Step one, size. The count of A cross A is the square of the size of A, so the square is sixteen and the size of A is four. Step two, elements. Since one comma four is in the product, both one and four belong to A; since three comma two is in it, three and two belong too. That is already four distinct elements, and there is no room for more, so A is exactly one, two, three, four.

Step three, the subset count. A cross A has sixteen pairs, and four comma one is genuinely one of them. Subsets that must contain it number two to the power fifteen, which is thirty two thousand seven hundred sixty eight.

Why fifteen in the exponent? Because fixing four comma one as always in freezes one decision, and each of the remaining fifteen pairs still gets a free, independent in-or-out choice. One frozen switch, fifteen live ones.
Now the advanced example. A runs from one to six, so A cross A has thirty six ordered pairs. Part a asks how many pairs satisfy x divides y.

Slice by the first coordinate, the same trick as our proof. For each x, the number of multiples of x inside one to six is the floor of six over x. That gives six, three, two, one, one, one as x runs from one to six, and the total is fourteen.

Part b asks for x divides y, or y divides x. By the symmetry of swapping x and y, the count of pairs with y dividing x is also fourteen. Inclusion exclusion says add the two counts and subtract the overlap: fourteen plus fourteen minus six is twenty two.

Why six for the overlap? Both conditions holding at once forces x equal to y, and there are exactly six such diagonal pairs, one one up to six six. The elegance is that a divisibility question became clean counting the instant we viewed the domain as A cross A.
Before we move to relations, let us armour-plate this subtopic against the mistakes that actually cost marks in the exam hall.
The single most common error: writing the count of A cross B as size of A plus size of B. It is always the product, never the sum.

The reason is structural: pairing is every-with-every, so counts multiply. Do one honest listing early in your preparation, with two elements in each set giving four pairs, and the muscle memory will protect you forever.

Second pitfall: treating a comma b and b comma a as identical. They are equal only when the two entries coincide. Reversing coordinates is the most exploited distractor on this topic, so always read the question carefully to see which set feeds the first slot.
Third, the one missing factor oversight. The number of subsets of A cross B is two raised to the product of the sizes, not two raised to their sum, and not the product itself.

Make it a two-stage habit: compute the number of pairs first, then raise two to that power. And keep one eye out for the empty set: if a problem sneaks in an empty A, the product is empty immediately, no pairing needed.

<whisper> Two speed moves to finish. When a question gives you the element count of A cross A, take the square root first to get the size of A, then read the actual elements off the listed pairs. And for common pairs of A cross B and B cross A, skip enumeration entirely: the answer is the square of the size of A intersect B.

segments.text: New subtopic: relations. The good news is that the hard work is already done, because a relation is built directly out of the Cartesian product we just mastered.

Picture the WhatsApp contact list on your phone. On one side sits the set of people you know; on the other, the set of phone numbers. Not every person is linked to every number; you have connected specific people to specific numbers. That hand-picked set of person-to-number links is exactly what mathematicians call a relation.

Here is the key realization. A cross B is the set of all possible ordered pairs, most of them meaningless. A relation R from A to B is simply any subset of A cross B, the meaningful portion you carve out. That is the whole definition, nothing more.

Or think of the full Mumbai local-train timetable, every train against every station, an enormous grid. A relation is the highlighter you run over it, say, trains that actually stop at Dadar. You have not created new trains; you have selected relevant pairs. Different highlighters, different rules, give different relations on the same grid.

The carving is done by a rule. If A is Riya, Aman and Sara, and B is their roll numbers, the rule is-assigned-roll-number picks out three specific pairs from the nine sitting in A cross B, and those three pairs are the relation.
Notation next. When the pair a comma b belongs to R, we say a is related to b, and write it compactly as a R b. When the pair is not in R, we write it with the crossed-out membership symbol.

Let this sink in: a relation is not some new exotic object with its own machinery. It is just a chosen portion of the grid you already understand, which is why everything we proved about the product transfers directly.
Three companion ideas travel everywhere with a relation, and one distinction among them is the most slippery point of the whole subtopic. Let us pin all three down.

The domain is the set of first coordinates that actually show up in R, the elements of A that get used. The range is the set of second coordinates that actually show up, the outputs in use. The codomain is the entire declared set B, whether or not every element of it gets used. In the contacts analogy, the domain is the people who actually have a number saved, and the range is the numbers actually in use.

The arrow diagram on the board makes this concrete. A holds one to four, B holds three to seven, and the rule y equals x plus two draws four arrows. Every left dot with an arrow leaving is in the domain; every right dot with an arrow arriving is in the range; and the element seven, circled in red, receives no arrow at all.

That circled seven is the slippery point. Codomain is the whole target set you declared; range is only the part the relation actually reaches. Range is always a subset of the codomain, and the two need not be equal. Say it as a slogan: range is reached, codomain is allowed.

A relation can be written three ways. Roster form spells out every ordered pair. Set-builder form states the rule, like y equals x plus two with memberships attached. And the arrow diagram draws the two sets as columns of dots with an arrow for each related pair. Remember: roster and arrow forms only work when the sets are finite; for infinite sets, set-builder is the only option.

Two extreme cases are perfectly legal. The empty relation, with no pairs at all, is a valid subset, and its domain and range are both empty. The universal relation, all of A cross B, is also valid, the one where everything is related to everything.

Finally, vocabulary you will meet constantly: a relation on a set A means a relation from A to itself, a subset of A cross A. And note that the domain is contained in A but need not be all of A; a relation is free to skip elements.

segments.text: Here is the compact formula card for relations. Every exam question on this subtopic is powered by the handful of lines now on the board.
The domain, written formally: the set of all a such that the pair a comma b sits in R for at least one b. It collects exactly the first coordinates in use, and it always sits inside A.
Mirror image for the range: all b such that some pair a comma b lies in R. Second coordinates in use, always sitting inside B.
The codomain needs no formula because it is simply B itself, the entire declared target. And the containment to remember: the range is always a subset of the codomain.

Now the headline count. If A has p elements and B has q, the product holds p q pairs, and a relation is any subset of it, so the number of relations from A to B is two raised to the power p q. Note the structure: p q counts pairs, and the power of two counts subsets.

Two corollaries. For a relation on A, a subset of A cross A, the count becomes two raised to the power, n of A squared. And since exactly one of those subsets is the empty relation, the number of non-empty relations is two to the p q, minus one.

Anchor the pattern in your mind as a chant: pairs count p q, relations count two to the p q. Subsets, so always a power of two. Whenever an option in an MCQ is not a power of two, it cannot be a relation count.
There is no single derivation for the definition of a relation, but three procedures carry every exam question, so let us drill each one.

Procedure one, rule to roster. First identify the playground, the sets A and B. Then apply the rule as a filter: with a rule like y equals x plus two, walk through each valid x in A, compute y, and keep the pair only if y lands inside B.

The discard step is where careless students bleed marks. A value of y produced by the rule but not lying in B is thrown away, no exceptions. Why? Because a relation lives inside A cross B, and any pair whose coordinate escapes the declared sets simply is not allowed in, no matter what the rule says.
Once the list is finished, the domain and range are read straight off it: distinct first coordinates give the domain, distinct second coordinates give the range.

Procedure two runs the other way, roster to set-builder. Spot the pattern linking each first coordinate to its second, is it y equals x plus one, does x divide y, is x plus y ten. Write the rule with quantified membership. Then verify both ways: every listed pair must satisfy the rule, and the rule must produce no pair you did not list.

Procedure three is the counting logic behind two to the p q, worth proving once so you never doubt it. A relation is a subset of A cross B, which has exactly p q ordered pairs. To build a subset, each of those p q pairs faces an independent yes or no decision, is this pair in R or not. Two choices per pair, made p q times independently, multiply to two raised to the p q.

Notice that this count includes both extremes, the empty relation where every answer is no, and the universal relation where every answer is yes. Subtract the single empty case and you get the count of non-empty relations, two to the p q minus one.

board_events.text: Example 1 (CBSE): R = {(x, y) : y = x + 2} on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
$x = 1 \Rightarrow y = 3$ ✓, $x = 2 \Rightarrow 4$ ✓, $x = 3 \Rightarrow 5$ ✓, $x = 4 \Rightarrow 6$ ✓, $x = 5 \Rightarrow 7 \notin A$ ✗, $x = 6 \Rightarrow 8 \notin A$ ✗
Domain $= \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$, Range $= \{3, 4, 5, 6\}$, Codomain $= A = \{1, \ldots, 6\}$.
5 and 6 are in A but NOT in the domain — domain ⊆ A need not be all of A.
Example 2 (JEE speed trap): n(A) = 3, n(B) = 4 — how many relations?
Wrong reflexes: $3 \times 4 = 12$ (that's the PAIR count) and $2^{3+4} = 128$ (added in the exponent).
Example 3 (JEE Main): R = {(x, y) : x, y ∈ ℤ, x² + y² = 25}
$25 = 0 + 25 = 25 + 0 = 9 + 16 = 16 + 9$ — squares available: $0, 9, 16, 25$. Attach ALL sign choices.
Geometrically: the 12 lattice points on a circle of radius 5. Domain = Range = $\{-5, -4, -3, 0, 3, 4, 5\}$ by $x \leftrightarrow y$ symmetry.
Example 4 (JEE Advanced): relations on A = {1, 2, 3} with AT LEAST ONE diagonal pair
Total relations $= 2^9 = 512$. "At least one" invites messy inclusion–exclusion — count the COMPLEMENT instead.
k forced pairs (in OR out) freeze k switches: count = 2^(n² − k).
Pitfalls — relations
Domain Left, Range Right (D-L, R-R) — never swap!
Codomain vs range: DECLARED vs REACHED. If asked for the range, do not just copy B — list the second coordinates that genuinely appear.
$pq$ vs $2^{pq}$: pairs vs relations — always exponentiate. And kill phantom pairs: check every output is actually in $B$.
"At least one …" ⇒ count the complement ("none of them") and subtract from $2^{pq}$ — almost always faster than inclusion–exclusion.
Mantra: relation = highlighted slice of A × B.

segments.text: Let us run the procedures on real questions. First a board staple: A is one to six, and R is defined by the rule y equals x plus two. We want roster form, domain, range and codomain.

Generate systematically. x equal to one gives y equal to three, in A, keep it. Two gives four, keep. Three gives five, keep. Four gives six, keep. But five gives seven, which is not in A, discard, and six gives eight, discard again. The filter step in action.
So the roster form has exactly four pairs: one three, two four, three five, and four six. Notice how the rule generated candidates, but membership in A had the final say.

Read the companions off the list. Domain, the first coordinates, is one, two, three, four. Range, the second coordinates, is three, four, five, six. Codomain is all of A, the whole declared set, one through six.

Here is the clean illustration worth remembering: five and six belong to A, yet the rule pushes their outputs out of the set, so they never appear as first coordinates. They are in A but not in the domain. The domain sits inside A but need not fill it.

Now the speed trap. A has three elements, B has four. How many relations from A to B, and how many are non-empty? The two reflex wrong answers are twelve, which is only the number of ordered pairs, and two to the seventh, one hundred twenty eight, from adding in the exponent instead of multiplying.

The correct move: relations are subsets of A cross B, so the count is two raised to three times four, that is two to the twelve, four thousand ninety six. The empty relation is one of these, so the non-empty count is four thousand ninety five.
Both wrong reflexes come from the same root, forgetting that a relation is a subset of A cross B. Anchor the two-step: multiply to count pairs, then exponentiate to count subsets.

Two richer examples. The first fuses relation-building with finding integer solutions: R is the set of integer pairs x comma y with x squared plus y squared equal to twenty five. We want roster form, domain and range.

Which squares can add to twenty five? The available squares are zero, nine, sixteen and twenty five, and the working combinations are twenty five plus zero, zero plus twenty five, nine plus sixteen, and sixteen plus nine. Since we are over the integers, every sign choice must be attached to each combination.

Writing them all out: zero with plus or minus five, plus or minus five with zero, plus or minus three with plus or minus four, and plus or minus four with plus or minus three. Count them carefully: twelve ordered pairs in total.

Geometrically these are exactly the twelve lattice points sitting on a circle of radius five. The domain and the range both come out as minus five, minus four, minus three, zero, three, four, five, and they coincide because the equation is symmetric when x and y swap roles.
Now the advanced counting question. On A equal to one, two, three, how many relations contain at least one of the diagonal pairs, one one, two two, or three three?

A relation on A is a subset of A cross A, which has nine pairs, so there are two to the ninth, five hundred twelve relations in total. Counting at least one of three directly invites messy inclusion exclusion, so we count the complement instead: relations containing none of the three diagonal pairs.

Force all three diagonal pairs out. That freezes three of the nine switches, leaving six pairs each free to be in or out, giving two to the sixth, sixty four such relations. Subtract from the total: five hundred twelve minus sixty four is four hundred forty eight.

The structural lesson: fixing k specific pairs, whether as must-be-in or must-be-out, freezes k of the independent yes-no switches, and the count becomes two raised to n squared minus k. Here we used it through the complement, and for at-least-one questions, the complement route is almost always faster.
Let us close the relations subtopic by naming the traps, because each of these has a dedicated distractor waiting in the MCQs.

Trap one, the domain-range swap: reading second coordinates as the domain or first coordinates as the range. Lock in the slogan, domain left, range right, inputs on the left, outputs on the right. It is the same order-matters trap from Cartesian products, wearing a new costume.

Trap two, confusing range with codomain. Codomain is the whole declared set B; range is only the part actually hit. If a question hands you B explicitly and asks for the range, do not just copy B down; list the second coordinates that genuinely appear.

Trap three, the counting confusion: p q is the number of pairs, two to the p q is the number of relations. Forgetting to exponentiate, or adding p plus q in the exponent, wrecks the count. And trap four, phantom pairs: a y generated by the rule that lies outside B must be excluded, so always check the output belongs to the target set.
Now the speed anchors. When some pairs are forced in or forced out, freeze them: each forced pair removes one factor of two, giving two to the power p q minus k for k forced pairs.
And for at-least-one conditions, count the complement, none of them, and subtract from two to the p q. That route is almost always faster than inclusion exclusion.
Keep the mantra with you as we head into functions: a relation is a highlighted slice of A cross B. Everything in the next subtopic is a special, disciplined kind of that slice.

segments.text: Final subtopic, and the star of the chapter: functions. You have met relations, any highlighted slice of A cross B. A function is a relation with discipline, a relation that obeys two strict promises, and those two promises are the whole idea.

<curious> Think of a snack vending machine. Each button is wired to deliver exactly one product. Two things are guaranteed: press a button and you always get something, no dead buttons, and you get one definite item, never maybe a samosa, maybe a Frooti.
Promise one is totality: every element of A has an image in B. No input is left unmapped, no dead buttons on the panel.
Promise two is single-valuedness: no element of A has more than one image. Each input gives one definite output, never a lottery.

Formally, a function f from A to B is a relation from A to B in which every element of A appears as the first coordinate of exactly one pair. The word exactly packs both promises: at least one pair means totality, at most one means single-valued.

Picture the Mumbai dabbawala system. Each tiffin must reach exactly one office address. A tiffin with no address is a failure, that violates promise one; a tiffin tagged with two addresses is chaos, violating promise two. But two different tiffins going to the same office is perfectly fine: many inputs sharing one output is allowed. What is forbidden is one input splitting into many outputs.

Compare with an ordinary relation, which is free to skip elements of A and free to send one element to several places. A function forbids both. So every function is a relation, but most relations are not functions.
With the definition in hand, let us set up the language and the one visual test you will use for the rest of your mathematical life.

The notation y equals f of x reads, y is the image of x under f. We call x the independent variable, the input we choose freely; y the dependent variable, determined by that choice; and f of x the value of f at x.

The three companions from relations sharpen for functions. The domain is now the entire set A, because promise one forces every element to be used. The codomain is still the declared target B. And the range is the set of images actually produced.
In symbols, the range of f is the set of all f of x as x runs over A, and it still sits inside the codomain B, possibly smaller than it.

For functions on real numbers there is a beautiful visual test. Draw the graph, then run vertical lines across it. If every vertical line meets the graph in at most one point, each x gives one y, and the graph is a function. On the left of the board, the parabola passes: the dashed line meets it once.

On the right, the circle fails: the dashed red line cuts it twice, one x giving two y values. That is why x squared plus y squared equals twenty five, the relation we listed earlier with its twelve lattice points, is a perfectly good relation but not a function.
Summarize the test in one line: vertical line meets the graph at most once, function. Meets it twice anywhere, not a function. You will apply this reflexively from now on.
Before the standard functions, some fine print. These small clauses are exactly where examiners hide the difference between full marks and half marks.

First, the square root convention. The square root symbol returns the non-negative root only. If it returned plus-or-minus, one input would have two outputs, breaking single-valuedness, so plus-or-minus root is not a function. Single-valued is non-negotiable.

Second, keep the asymmetry straight: many-to-one is allowed, several inputs may share an output; one-to-many is banned. And on the totality side, if even one element of A has no image, the relation is not a function on A; at best it is a function on the smaller set of mapped elements.

Third, the natural domain convention. When a rule like f of x equals one over x is given without a stated domain, the domain is taken to be all real x for which the rule makes sense. For one over x that is all reals except zero, since division by zero is meaningless.

Fourth, equality of functions. Two functions f and g are equal if and only if they have the same domain, and f of x equals g of x for every x in that domain. Two conditions, and the domain condition is the one students forget.

The consequence is striking: the same rule on a different domain gives a different function. f of x equals x on all of R, and g of x equals x on the interval zero to one, share the formula but are not equal, because their domains differ.

Finally, two vocabulary items. If the range of f sits inside the reals, f is called real-valued. If additionally the domain also sits inside the reals, f is a real function. Everything in the coming graph work is about real functions.

segments.text: Two formula clusters power the rest of this subtopic: the counting formula for functions, and the algebra of real functions with its domain bookkeeping.
If A has p elements and B has q elements, the number of functions from A to B is q raised to the power p, the size of B raised to the size of A.

Here is the logic. Each of the p inputs must be assigned exactly one of the q outputs, and the choices are independent, so q multiplied by itself p times. There is no yes-no per pair here, that gave two to the p q for relations. It is one choice of output per input, which is why the base is q and the exponent is p, and why functions are far fewer than relations.

Now the algebra. Real functions can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and scaled pointwise: f plus minus g at x is f of x plus minus g of x, the product at x is f of x times g of x, and alpha f at x is alpha times f of x.
The quotient works the same way, f over g at x is f of x divided by g of x, but only wherever g of x is non-zero, because division by zero is undefined.

The domain bookkeeping is where marks live. For sum, difference and product, the domain is the intersection of the two domains, since both functions must be defined to combine them. For the quotient, take that intersection and then remove every point where g vanishes. That extra removal is the step students forget.
And to kill the classic base-exponent swap forever, chant it: outputs to the power of inputs, q to the p, never p to the q.

Now the standard real functions, the Class eleven zoo. These are the graphs every student must be able to sketch on sight, because once you can picture a graph, its domain and range fall out by inspection.
First, the identity function, f of x equals x. Its graph is the forty five degree line through the origin: every input maps to itself. Domain all reals, range all reals.

Second, the constant function, f of x equals c. A horizontal line at height c: every input lands on the single value c, so the range is just the one-element set containing c, while the domain is still all reals.
Study the four graphs on the board and practice the projection trick: the shadow a graph casts on the x axis is its domain, and the shadow on the y axis is its range. We will use this constantly.

Third, the modulus function, f of x equals the absolute value of x. A symmetric V with its vertex at the origin, falling with slope minus one on the left and rising with slope plus one on the right. It never dips below the x axis, so the range is zero to infinity, with zero included.

Fourth, the polynomial family, with x squared as the flagship: an upward parabola with vertex at the origin. An even degree polynomial like this never reaches negative values, so its range is zero to infinity, a concrete instance of the rule that the range depends on the degree. And its cousin, the rational function p of x over q of x, is defined everywhere except where the denominator vanishes.
The takeaway slogan: a function's graph is its fingerprint. Learn the fingerprints in this zoo and most domain-range questions become thirty second reads instead of computations.
Two more zoo members remain, and they are the two examiners love most, because both have jumps and both punish sloppy reading.

The signum function of x has three flat pieces: minus one for negative x, zero exactly at zero, and plus one for positive x, with jumps at the origin. Its whole range is just the three values minus one, zero and one.

The greatest integer function, bracket x, returns the largest integer that does not exceed x. Its graph is a left-closed staircase: on each interval from n up to but not including n plus one, the value is the integer n. The filled dot, included, sits at the left end of each step, the open dot, excluded, at the right. The range is all integers.
Look at the two graphs on the board and note the open and filled dots carefully; they mark which endpoint each step actually attains, and MCQs test exactly this.

The classic negative-number trap: bracket of minus two point three is minus three, not minus two. The integers not exceeding minus two point three are minus three, minus four and so on, and the greatest of them is minus three. The function rounds down toward minus infinity; it never just drops the decimal.

Now the general graph-reading skill. Project the curve onto the axes: the shadow it casts on the x axis is the domain, every x value the graph covers, and the shadow on the y axis is the range, every y value it attains. And always run the vertical line test first to confirm the picture is a function at all.

One JEE companion beyond the Class eleven core: the fractional part of x, x minus bracket x, strips off the integer part. It is a sawtooth with range from zero up to but not including one, and it is studied alongside the greatest integer function in the Class twelve and JEE toolkit.

segments.text: Time for worked examples. First, the bread-and-butter check: A is one to four, B is two, three, five, seven, and R contains the pairs one two, two three, three two, and four five. Is R a function from A to B?

Check promise one, totality. The first coordinates appearing are one, two, three and four, so every element of A is present, no dead buttons. Check promise two, single-valuedness. No first coordinate repeats, so no input has two images. Both promises hold.
Notice the output two is shared by inputs one and three. That is many-to-one, which is perfectly allowed, remember the two tiffins going to the same office. So yes, R is a function.
The domain is all of A, one through four, forced by promise one. The range is the set of distinct images: two, three and five.
And look at seven: it belongs to B but is never hit by any arrow. It sits in the codomain, not in the range, our slippery distinction showing up in an actual answer.
Now the speed trap. A has three elements, B has four. How many functions from A to B? Three reflex wrong answers compete here, so slow down for two seconds.
The correct base is the number of choices per input, which is q, and the exponent is the number of inputs, p. So the count is four cubed, sixty four.

The wrong reflexes: two to the twelve, four thousand ninety six, counts relations, not functions. Three to the four, eighty one, swaps base and exponent, assigning the sets backwards. And three times four, twelve, is merely the pair count. The mnemonic that kills the swap: each input picks an output, so outputs are the base and inputs are the exponent.
Domain-finding is guaranteed exam territory, so let us do it twice: once for a single formula, once for combined functions where the bookkeeping bites.
First function: the square root of x minus two, all divided by x minus five. Two danger sources live in this formula, and both must be respected simultaneously.

Danger one, the even root: the radicand x minus two must be at least zero, so x is at least two. Danger two, the denominator: x minus five must not be zero, so x is not five. The rule must survive both hurdles at once, so we intersect the conditions.
The intersection is the ray from two to infinity, with the single point five punched out, written as two to five, closed at two and open at five, union five to infinity.

Two subtleties worth voicing. The point x equal to two stays in, because the square root of zero is zero, which is perfectly fine; only the denominator is forbidden to vanish. And five is removed as a single punched-out point, splitting the ray into two intervals.
Now the advanced version: f of x is x squared, g of x is the square root of four minus x squared. We want f plus g, f times g, and f over g, each with its exact domain.

Pin down the individual domains first. f is a polynomial, defined on all reals. For g, we need four minus x squared at least zero, so x squared at most four, giving x between minus two and two inclusive. Sum and product need both functions defined, so their domain is the intersection, the closed interval minus two to two.

The quotient is where marks are lost. Start from that closed interval, then remove the points where g vanishes: the root of four minus x squared is zero exactly at x equal to plus and minus two, so both endpoints are punched out, and the domain of f over g is the open interval minus two to two. The deep point: sum and product keep the closed interval, but the quotient must shed the zeros of g, and forgetting to exclude the endpoints is the single most common error here.

One final worked example, chosen because it welds algebra to graph reading: f of x equals the absolute value of x minus two, on all reals. Describe the graph, state domain and range, evaluate f of five, and solve f of x equals three.

Part a, the graph. The plain modulus is a V with vertex at the origin. Replacing x by x minus two slides the whole V right by two units, so our graph is a V with vertex at the point two comma zero, arms rising with slopes plus and minus one. This shift rule, x goes to x minus a slides right by a, is a graph-transformation tool you will reuse all year.

Part b, domain and range, by projection. The graph spans every x, so the domain is all reals. It never drops below the x axis and touches zero exactly at x equal to two, so the range is zero to infinity, zero included.
Say the projection reasoning out loud once: shadow on the x axis, everything, shadow on the y axis, from zero upward. That is the whole computation.
Part c, evaluation. f of five is the absolute value of five minus two, the absolute value of three, which is three.

Part d, the equation. Absolute value of x minus two equals three splits into two linear cases: x minus two equals three, giving x equal to five, or x minus two equals minus three, giving x equal to minus one. Two solutions.

And here is the beauty: the graph predicted this. A horizontal line at height three cuts the V in exactly two points, one on each arm, and those two points sit precisely at x equal to five and x equal to minus one. When algebra and the picture agree, you know you are right.
The last set of traps, and these are the ones that decide ranks, because functions questions are guaranteed scorers if you dodge them.
Trap one is philosophical: the function rule constrains inputs, each domain element to one image, not outputs.

So never reject a candidate function just because some codomain element goes unused, or because an output value repeats. Many inputs sharing an output is fine; one input with two outputs is fatal. Check the input side, always.

Trap two is the counting triangle: relations are two to the p q, functions are q to the p, with outputs as base and inputs as exponent. Swapping to p to the q is the most tested distractor on the topic, so keep the chant running, outputs to the power of inputs.

Trap three, strict versus non-strict inequalities in domains. An even root allows its radicand to equal zero, closed bracket. A denominator forbids zero, open. And when a radical sits inside a denominator, like one over root of something, the inside must be strictly positive, both conditions at once.

Trap four, the quotient domain. Domain of f over g is the intersection of the two domains minus the zeros of g. Endpoints that survive in the sum often vanish in the quotient, exactly as our plus-minus-two example showed.

And a final memory pair: the signum range is the three-element set minus one, zero, one, while the modulus range is the interval zero to infinity. Examiners swap these two constantly, so keep them welded to their graphs, three flat steps versus the V.
